newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German Feb unemployment report.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German Feb unemployment report.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to a report from the Federal Labour Office showing that German seasonally adjusted unemployment increased 5,000 to 4.316 million. On an unadjusted basis, the unemployment rate stood at 12.2 percent with 4.672 million out of work.

UWE ANGENENDT, BHF-BANK: This confirms our estimation that the rise in unemployment was caused by special factors in January such as cold weather. We believe that we will see a signficant reduction in the unemployment figures in March. We expect a figure of 4.5 million in March. All in all, the unemployment rate remains high for Germany. For all of 1996, we expect 4.2 million people. we have therefore increased our deficit estimation from 3.0 percent to 3.3 percent.

HUW ROBERTS OF NATWEST: The number is much better than we had all been expecting. The labour mrket remains extremely weak as far as we can tell. There are still quite a few structural problems that will act as a drag on a cyclical bounce.

That means that others will be able to extract a greater compromise in EMU negotiations. This is a slightly negative from a Bund market perspective. The big question is how Bunds will react with Treasuries. I would not be surprised if we tested the downside on the near term. But at end of the day, I would guess that is still some way away. In the near term, the news flow should be quiet friendly for Bunds."

JOERG KRAEMER, MERRILL LYNCH: "My feeling is that the number is quiet low. The trend is still uwpards. Germany's bargaining position for keeping Italy out of EMU is weakened. Therefore there will be broad EMU rather than core EMU.

FRANK SCHROEDER, TRINKAUS & BURKHARDT: "The rise is lower than had been feared. We should have reached the peak of unemployment now and we expect a clear fall in March due to seasonal factors and because construction workers laid off in December due to new rules on bad weather pay are likely to be rehired now. But we are sceptical about the government's assumption that unemployment will average 4.2 million in 1997, we see it higher by about 100,000 because not all construction workers laid off in December will be hired back. Rationalisation and shifts of production abroad will continue and expected GDP growth of 2.0 to 2.5 percent is not high enough to give strong impetus to employment. Also, there's a silent reserve of people who are not registered as unemployed but will reenter the labour market as soon as employment prospects improve, thereby slowing the fall in the jobless numbers. We see Germany's budget deficit at 3.2 percent in 1997 but expect Germany will still be able to join European monetary union.
